triage.name: Collapsed Lung
triage.reason: Acute presentation with dyspnea and chest pain; diagnosis reachable by exam and imaging, with important mimics.

age.peak: bimodal: 20s (spontaneous pneumothorax) and 60s (secondary to lung disease)

demographics: Spontaneous pneumothorax is more common in males, especially tall, thin young men
Secondary pneumothorax is more common in older adults with underlying lung disease
Atelectasis is common in hospitalized or postoperative patients of any age

risk_factors.text: Tall, thin body habitus in a young male
Underlying lung disease such as COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis, or interstitial lung disease
Recent chest trauma or rib fracture
Marfan syndrome or other connective tissue disease

family_history: Spontaneous pneumothorax in a family member
social_history: Recent air travel or scuba diving (for pneumothorax)

chief_complaints.text: I suddenly felt a sharp pain in my chest
It hurts when I take a deep breath

hpi.onset: Sudden for pneumothorax; gradual or insidious for atelectasis
hpi.duration: Minutes to hours for pneumothorax; hours to days for atelectasis
hpi.progression: Pneumothorax: pain and breathlessness peak within minutes to hours and may plateau. Atelectasis: symptoms develop over hours to days and worsen as more lung collapses.
hpi.location: One side of the chest, often the same side as the collapsed lung
hpi.radiation: May radiate to the shoulder or back on the affected side
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; 6–9/10 for pneumothorax, milder for atelectasis

associated_symptoms.text: Feeling of tightness in the chest
Fever (if due to pneumonia or atelectasis)

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain that is pressure-like and radiates to the jaw or arm

argues_against: Productive cough with fever suggests pneumonia rather than primary pneumothorax

negatives: Chest pressure radiating to jaw or arm
argues_against: Pressure-like chest pain radiating to jaw suggests acute coronary syndrome
Weight loss and night sweats suggest malignancy or tuberculosis

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may have vague chest pain, abdominal pain, or irritability; infants may present with tachypnea and grunting.
Older adults may have milder pain and more breathlessness, and may not mount a fever or tachycardia.
Pregnancy can mask or alter symptoms; dyspnea is common, and chest pain may be attributed to other causes.

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences, no distress
general.moderate: Mild distress, prefers sitting upright, speaks in full sentences but pauses with deep breaths
general.severe: Obvious respiratory distress, sitting upright, using accessory muscles, speaks in short phrases
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, agitated or lethargic, diaphoretic, unable to speak in full sentences, may be hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Auscultate both lung fields at the apices, mid-lung, and bases while comparing sides
findings.finding: Decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the chest wall over the affected side
findings.finding: Chest wall tenderness, especially after trauma

findings.maneuver: Percuss the chest on both sides from apex to base
findings.finding: Hyperresonance or tympany over the affected side (pneumothorax)

findings.maneuver: Percuss the chest on both sides from apex to base
findings.finding: Dullness over the affected area (atelectasis or pleural effusion)

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to say 'ninety-nine' while palpating both sides of the chest
findings.finding: Decreased tactile fremitus on the affected side

findings.maneuver: Palpate the trachea at the suprasternal notch and compare its position with midline
findings.finding: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side (tension pneumothorax) or toward the affected side (atelectasis)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular veins with the patient at 30–45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure (tension pneumothorax with impaired venous return)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the neck, supraclavicular area, and chest wall
Observe the patient's breathing at rest
findings.finding: Use of accessory muscles of respiration, nasal flaring, or intercostal retractions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, oral mucosa, and nail beds
Auscultate the heart at the apex and base
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur, rub, or gallop

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate both calves for asymmetry, swelling, or tenderness
findings.finding: No unilateral calf swelling or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Assess for focal infectious signs (productive cough, consolidation, rash)
findings.finding: No focal signs of pneumonia or systemic infection

labs.caveat: A normal white count is common in primary spontaneous pneumothorax; leukocytosis suggests an underlying pneumonia, empyema, or other infection rather than the collapse itself.
Elevated only with shock or severe hypoperfusion, as in tension pneumothorax.
Helps separate decompensated heart failure from a primary lung problem when acute dyspnea is the main complaint.
Nonspecific; may be elevated in pneumothorax and many other acute illnesses. Useful mainly to rule out pulmonary embolism when the chest x-ray is normal or the presentation is atypical.
Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; acidosis indicates respiratory failure or a tension pneumothorax.
Low from hyperventilation; a rising PaCO2 in a breathless patient signals impending respiratory failure.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before chest x-ray or CT.

findings.finding: Right axis deviation or rightward shift in tension pneumothorax
Low-voltage QRS complexes from increased air between the heart and the electrodes
T-wave inversion in the precordial leads
ST-segment elevation or depression mimicking acute coronary syndrome

findings.text: Visible pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it
Collapsed or compressed lung on the affected side
Hyperlucent hemithorax on the affected side
Mediastinal shift away from the affected side (tension pneumothorax)
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side (tension pneumothorax)
Deep sulcus sign on a supine film
Subcutaneous emphysema
Rib fractures or other trauma
Patchy opacity, volume loss, and displacement of fissures (atelectasis)
No pneumothorax seen (false negative in a small or anterior collection)

imaging.preferred_when: When the chest x-ray is equivocal, or to define the size, cause, and underlying lung disease

findings.text: Air in the pleural space with a visible visceral pleural edge
Underlying emphysema, bullae, or blebs
Lung collapse with mediastinal shift in tension pneumothorax
Endobronchial obstruction or mass causing atelectasis
Pleural effusion or empyema

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside assessment in the emergency department or ICU; avoids radiation

findings.text: Absent lung sliding
Absent B-lines and a lung point
A-lines with no comet-tail artifact

imaging.preferred_when: When pulmonary embolism is the leading alternative diagnosis

findings.text: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery (pulmonary embolism)
Incidental pneumothorax or pleural air

initial.why: First-line test to confirm pneumothorax and estimate its size
Rules out pregnancy before chest x-ray or CT
Looks for infection or anemia when pneumonia, empyema, or trauma is suspected
initial.only_if: fever, productive cough, or suspected infection

initial.why: Baseline electrolytes and renal function before procedures or contrast
initial.only_if: moderate to severe illness or planned intervention

initial.why: Assesses ventilation and acid-base status in severe dyspnea or suspected respiratory failure
initial.only_if: severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, or suspected respiratory failure

confirmatory.why: Defines the cause and extent when the chest x-ray is equivocal or underlying lung disease is suspected
confirmatory.only_if: chest x-ray is equivocal or a secondary cause is suspected

supporting.why: Rapid bedside confirmation when radiography is delayed or unavailable
Evaluates for pulmonary embolism when that is the leading alternative
Helps distinguish heart failure from a primary lung cause of dyspnea
Screens for pulmonary embolism when the chest x-ray is normal and the presentation is atypical
supporting.only_if: pulmonary embolism is suspected and the chest x-ray is normal

decision_points: Pregnancy test before chest x-ray or CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; decompress immediately without waiting for imaging
Chest x-ray first; CT when the film is equivocal or an underlying cause is suspected
Consider pulmonary embolism when the chest x-ray is normal and dyspnea is unexplained

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with tachycardia and hypoxemia can look identical to a spontaneous pneumothorax.
differential.trigger: Acute dyspnea with a normal chest x-ray, or with risk factors such as recent immobility, surgery, or malignancy

history: Sudden onset of dyspnea, often without chest wall pain
Recent surgery, immobility, long travel, or active cancer
Prior venous thromboembolism
Hemoptysis
exam: Tachycardia and tachypnea with clear, symmetric breath sounds
Unilateral calf swelling or tenderness
Signs of right heart strain in massive embolism
labs: Elevated troponin or BNP with right ventricular strain
imaging: Chest x-ray is usually normal or shows nonspecific findings, not a pleural line
CT pulmonary angiogram shows a filling defect in a pulmonary artery
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation
T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Acute chest pain with dyspnea and tachycardia is a common presentation of myocardial ischemia, and pneumothorax can even mimic it on ECG.
differential.trigger: Pressure-like chest pain, diaphoresis, or cardiovascular risk factors in an older adult

history: Pressure-like or squeezing chest pain
Pain radiating to the jaw, neck, or left arm
Exertional onset or relief with rest
Nausea and diaphoresis
exam: Symmetric breath sounds
No hyperresonance or tracheal deviation
New murmur or signs of heart failure
imaging: Chest x-ray without a pleural line
Echocardiography showing regional wall motion abnormality
ecg: T-wave inversion in a coronary distribution

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, and focal decreased breath sounds with dullness can resemble atelectasis or a collapsed lung.

history: Productive cough with fever and chills
Gradual onset over days
Recent upper respiratory infection
exam: Fever and tachypnea
Dullness to percussion with increased tactile fremitus
Crackles or bronchial breath sounds over the affected area
imaging: Lobar or patchy consolidation on chest x-ray

differential.name: Pleural effusion
differential.why_considered: Dyspnea with decreased breath sounds and dullness on the affected side can be mistaken for a collapsed lung.

history: Gradual onset of dyspnea
History of heart failure, malignancy, or infection
Pleuritic pain that improves when the effusion is large
exam: Dullness to percussion at the base
Decreased tactile fremitus
Tracheal deviation toward the affected side if massive
labs: BNP elevated if due to heart failure
Pleural fluid analysis shows exudate or transudate
imaging: Blunting of the costophrenic angle or meniscus sign on chest x-ray

differential.name: Atelectasis
differential.why_considered: Partial lung collapse from mucus plugging or compression is a direct form of collapsed lung and can present with mild dyspnea and focal decreased breath sounds.

history: Recent surgery, prolonged bed rest, or mechanical ventilation
Gradual onset over hours to days
History of asthma, COPD, or cystic fibrosis
exam: Dullness to percussion over the affected area
Decreased breath sounds with crackles
Tracheal deviation toward the affected side if severe
imaging: Patchy opacity with volume loss and fissure displacement on chest x-ray
CT shows collapsed lung with airway obstruction or external compression
No pleural line or air in the pleural space

differential.name: Pneumothorax (spontaneous)
differential.why_considered: This is the primary form of collapsed lung and must be distinguished from other causes of acute dyspnea and chest pain.

history: Sudden onset of sharp, pleuritic chest pain
Tall, thin young male or known lung disease
Prior pneumothorax
exam: Hyperresonance to percussion on the affected side
Decreased or absent breath sounds
Subcutaneous emphysema
imaging: Visible pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it on chest x-ray

differential.name: Tension pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: A life-threatening form of collapsed lung with hemodynamic compromise that must be recognized clinically without waiting for imaging.
differential.trigger: Hypotension, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side in a patient with acute dyspnea

history: Rapidly worsening dyspnea
Recent chest trauma or positive-pressure ventilation
Chest pain followed by cardiovascular collapse
exam: Hypotension and tachycardia
Distended neck veins
Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side
imaging: Chest x-ray shows mediastinal shift away from the affected side and a deep sulcus

severity.mild: Small pneumothorax or limited atelectasis; minimal symptoms, no distress, normal vital signs, oxygen saturation above 94% on room air
severity.moderate: Larger pneumothorax or significant atelectasis; dyspnea and pleuritic pain, mild tachycardia and tachypnea, oxygen saturation 90–94%
severity.severe: Large pneumothorax or extensive atelectasis with respiratory distress, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation below 90%, and hemodynamic stability maintained
severity.critical: Tension pneumothorax or respiratory failure with hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation, altered mental status, or need for immediate decompression

red_flags.finding: Hypotension with distended neck veins and tracheal deviation away from the affected side
red_flags.meaning: Tension pneumothorax; decompress immediately without waiting for imaging

red_flags.finding: Oxygen saturation below 90% on room air or increasing oxygen requirement
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoxemia; needs urgent intervention and monitoring
Cerebral hypoperfusion or severe hypoxemia; assess for tension pneumothorax and respiratory failure

red_flags.finding: Subcutaneous emphysema spreading to the neck and face
red_flags.meaning: Air tracking from the pleural space; may indicate a larger leak or barotrauma

red_flags.finding: Rapidly increasing dyspnea after chest trauma or positive-pressure ventilation
red_flags.meaning: Expanding pneumothorax; high risk of tension physiology

complications.name: Tension pneumothorax
clues: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side

complications.name: Recurrent pneumothorax
clues: Sudden return of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea
New pleural line on chest x-ray

complications.name: Persistent air leak
clues: Continued air bubbling from a chest tube
Failure of the lung to re-expand

complications.name: Empyema
clues: Pleural fluid with low pH and positive cultures

complications.name: Bronchopleural fistula
clues: History of necrotizing pneumonia or surgery

special_populations.differences: May present with vague chest or abdominal pain, irritability, or tachypnea without localizing findings; infants may have grunting and poor feeding. Neonatal pneumothorax can occur spontaneously or with respiratory distress syndrome.

Often have underlying COPD or interstitial lung disease; symptoms may be milder but the risk of respiratory failure and death is higher. A secondary pneumothorax in an older adult is more dangerous than a primary spontaneous one in a young person.
Dyspnea is common in pregnancy and may delay diagnosis. Chest x-ray with abdominal shielding is safe when indicated; treatment principles are similar but coordination with obstetrics is important.
Higher risk of infectious causes such as Pneumocystis pneumonia leading to pneumothorax; consider atypical infections and malignancy in the differential.
May have reduced baseline lung volumes and oxygen reserve, so a smaller pneumothorax can cause more significant hypoxemia; physical exam findings may be harder to elicit.

key_questions.question: When did the pain or shortness of breath start, and how fast did it come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset over minutes to hours suggests pneumothorax; gradual onset over hours to days suggests atelectasis

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it radiate anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: One-sided sharp chest pain that may radiate to the shoulder or back on the affected side

key_questions.question: What makes the pain worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with deep breathing, coughing, or movement (pleuritic)

key_questions.question: Are you more short of breath than usual, and is it getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive dyspnea; rapidly worsening breathlessness raises concern for tension pneumothorax

key_questions.question: Have you had a collapsed lung or pneumothorax before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior pneumothorax strongly increases the likelihood of recurrence

key_questions.question: Do you have any lung disease such as COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis, or interstitial lung disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Underlying lung disease points to secondary pneumothorax and a more dangerous course

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent chest injury, chest or abdominal surgery, or been on a breathing machine?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma, recent surgery, or mechanical ventilation are common causes of a collapsed lung

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or have you ever smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking is a strong risk factor for spontaneous pneumothorax

key_questions.question: Have you recently flown or been scuba diving?
Do you have a cough, fever, or are you coughing up sputum or blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Productive cough and fever suggest pneumonia or atelectasis rather than primary pneumothorax

key_questions.question: Have you had any weight loss, night sweats, or been around anyone with tuberculosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Constitutional symptoms raise concern for malignancy or tuberculosis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Must be excluded before chest x-ray or CT in anyone who could be pregnant

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a history of collapsed lung or pneumothorax?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of spontaneous pneumothorax or connective tissue disease

reasoning_points: Sudden onset of sharp, one-sided pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea
Risk factors such as smoking, tall thin body habitus, underlying lung disease, recent trauma, surgery, or mechanical ventilation
Decreased or absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion on the affected side
Tachycardia and tachypnea with hypoxemia on pulse oximetry
Chest x-ray showing a visible pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it, or patchy opacity with volume loss for atelectasis
Tension pneumothorax considered and excluded when hypotension, distended neck veins, or tracheal deviation are present
Pregnancy excluded before imaging when applicable
Alternative diagnoses such as pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome, and pneumonia considered and addressed

easy: Tall, thin young male smoker with sudden sharp one-sided chest pain and dyspnea
Decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side
Chest x-ray clearly shows a pleural line with absent lung markings
medium: Older adult with COPD and milder pain but significant breathlessness
Small pneumothorax with subtle exam findings and a less obvious pleural line on chest x-ray
Postoperative patient with gradual dyspnea and focal decreased breath sounds due to atelectasis
Woman of reproductive age with chest pain requiring pregnancy testing before imaging
hard: Tension pneumothorax with hypotension and distended neck veins requiring immediate decompression before imaging
Patient on mechanical ventilation with sudden desaturation and rising airway pressures
Chest x-ray equivocal or normal in a small anterior pneumothorax, requiring CT or ultrasound
Pneumothorax mimicking acute coronary syndrome on ECG with ST changes
Child or infant with vague chest or abdominal pain, irritability, and tachypnea without localizing findings
